Here’s how the loop works:

1.   Track outcomes. Trace production incidents and rollbacks back to the commits and reviews behind them.
2.   Learn from the data. Combine those outcomes with LLM analysis, static checks, and ML signals into one risk score per change.
3.   Automate selectively. Auto-approve the lowest-risk 30–50% of changes. Pick a conservative, balanced, or aggressive policy. Risky or uncertain changes still go to a human.
4.   Keep improving. Track incidents, false approvals, and overrides. Then tighten or loosen the policy as real data comes in.

The result? Your reviewers stop reading every line of every diff. Instead, they give their full attention to the 50–70% of changes that actually carry risk.

## Risk inside the diff, not just per PR [...] LiveReview follows the approach behind Meta’s internal AI review system, RADAR. The idea is simple: score every change for risk, fast-track the safe ones, and route the risky ones to the right reviewers.

At Meta, this approach led to:

   50× fewer production incidents
   3× fewer rollbacks
   35% faster reviews

LiveReview brings the same idea to any team, on any git provider. Self-hosted, and free.

Today we are launching LiveReview: a risk-aware code review system built to fix exactly that.

## LiveReview auto-approves your safest 30-50% of pull requests [...] Every pull request gets a risk score. The lowest-risk 30-50% are approved automatically. The rest go to the right human, in the right order, ranked by how much they actually matter.

## How LiveReview differs from other AI reviewers

Most tools in this space pick one of two jobs: find issues, or check style. LiveReview is built to be the layer that decides whether a human needs to look at all, and ranks what matters when they do.

Here is what actually changes when you compare LiveReview against CodeRabbit, Greptile, SonarQube, Claude Code review, GitHub Copilot review, and Cursor Bugbot, feature by feature, not by marketing claim: [...] A security-first team can block on any security finding at all. A fast-moving startup can block only on correctness and UX bugs, and let style debt through for now. Both are one `jq` expression against the same findings document, whether the review came from the web UI, `git-lrc`, CI/CD, or the API.

results.title: How auto-approving low-risk PRs with AI cut our lead time by 74% · Ona
results.content:
We spent two weeks tracking which PRs the agent reviewed where the human reviewer added nothing beyond approval. The pattern was consistent: small changes, no sensitive areas touched, tests passing, no infrastructure modifications. So we wrote a policy.

## The policy

Two principles guided the Low-Risk Change Policy.

First, engineers cannot self-classify a change as low-risk. An Ona Automation evaluates every PR against objective criteria automatically, which removes the temptation to game the system and makes the boundary auditable.

Second, the AI agent reviews every PR regardless of classification. The question is not whether the agent reviews, but whether a human also needs to.

### The six criteria

A change qualifies as low-risk only if it meets all of the following: [...] 1. Fewer than 1,000 lines changed (additions and deletions combined)
2. No protobuf changes added or modified
3. No database migrations added or modified
4. No infrastructure or CI configuration changes
5. No authentication or authorization logic changes
6. No audit logging or monitoring changes

If any single criterion is not met, the change is routed to human review.

### How the review works

When a pull request is opened, the AI agent reviews it in an isolated environment with independent context. It evaluates the change against the low-risk criteria and code quality, then posts a structured comment:

Approved. The change meets all low-risk criteria. The comment explains the reasoning for each criterion. [...] The policy also changed how engineers write PRs. Large, unfocused changes are more likely to trip the criteria and get routed to human review, so engineers naturally gravitate toward smaller, focused PRs. That is a win for everyone: smaller PRs are easier for humans to review, easier for the agent to review, and faster to ship.

Faster approval shortens lead time, which increases deploy frequency, which shrinks batch sizes, which lowers risk per change. DORA research describes this virtuous cycle, and we got there by removing the review bottleneck rather than adding more reviewers.

## What we learned

Start by observing, not by deciding. We did not start with a policy. We watched which PRs humans rubber-stamped, and the policy codified what we saw.
